transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Skyline Head of ML), Raj Patel (Skyline CTO), Sophie Turner (Skyline Data Eng)

Summary: Quick review of the latest quality eval runs (baseline vs tuned prompts), discussed a small regression on customer-support intent, went over guardrail insertion strategy, agreed to run a larger batch for regression detection and share SOC2/KMS artefacts. Next steps captured.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, can you hear us okay?
[00:03] Laura Kim: Yep, loud and clear, thanks.
[00:07] Maya Chen: Great. Diego and I will run through the quality runs you sent and then open it up for questions. main goal is to identify the regression you flagged on support intent and make sure the guardrails don't drop recall for clinical intent.
[00:20] Diego Martinez: Cool, i pulled the eval sheet earlier this morning, i ran the tuned-prompts against the baseline and there are two things to call out — overall macro-F1 up 2.3 points but that support intent we saw before dropped precision by about 6%. could be prompt phrasing or temperature.
[00:37] Sophie Turner: Quick q — when you say tuned prompts, is that the set we edited last wednesday? we added the clarifier line and lowered max tokens.
[00:45] Diego Martinez: yeah that's the set. we inserted the clarifier and tightened the few-shot examples to prefer conservative answers. that change helped the hallucination rate but looks like it made the model more likely to fall back to generic help text for support categories.
[01:02] Raj Patel: timeline questions: we need to decide if we go hosted or dedicated. security is a showstopper for patient data, so dedicated with VPC peering would be ideal, but cost matters. what are the latency SLA numbers we can hit in dedicated?
[01:18] Maya Chen: good question. on dedicated we typically see p95 generation latency in the 120-220ms range for the sequences you're testing when using gpus similar to A100-class, but that depends on batch config and KV cache hit rates. for strict p50/p95 you can tune batching and enable prefix cache.
[01:34] Laura Kim: can you clarify kv cache? sometimes our infra folks call it the key-value cache, other docs say KV store, just want to make sure we're aligned.
[01:40] Diego Martinez: yeah kv = key-value cache, it's the attention cache we persist between tokens — we might have had a transcription typo on earlier notes calling it k-v stash or something. that cache is what gives you lower per-token compute on long sessions.
[01:55] Sophie Turner: On the security side, are you able to support customer-managed KMS? we have to keep keys in our HSM for PHI data.
[02:02] Maya Chen: yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with your HSM via our KMS connector. we'll send the SOC2/KMS doc set after the call.
[02:12] Raj Patel: great. also need RBAC and audit logs retention policy. what are default retention windows?
[02:18] Diego Martinez: audit logs are by default 90 days in hosted, but on Dedicated or Private you can configure retention longer and export to your SIEM. we can share the audit log schema and sample export.
[02:29] Laura Kim: back to quality — the regression on support intent is the biggest risk to user experience. can we walk through a couple of failure examples?
[02:36] Diego Martinez: sure, i pulled three representative cases. example 1: user asks 'my claim was denied, how do i appeal' — baseline returned step-by-step appeal instructions; tuned prompts returned a generic 'contact support' note with no steps. it looks like the guardrail clarity pushed it to safe fallback.
[03:00] Sophie Turner: that maps to our label set where support intent needs procedural outputs.
[03:05] Diego Martinez: example 2: clinical question about medication dosing — baseline had acceptable conservative answer, tuned prompt tightened hallucination filters and actually improved safety. so it's mixed.
[03:17] Maya Chen: sounds like we need a more surgical guardrail: keep conservative hallucination filters but add intent-specific prompt anchors that favour procedural templates for support-type intents.
[03:27] Raj Patel: is that feasible without a model change? like can we handle that at prompt-level and routing?
[03:33] Diego Martinez: yes, two knobs: prompt templates per intent and routing to a slightly different model variant or temperature. we can also do post-generation reranking with a domain-specific classifier to boost answers that match the procedural template.
[03:47] Laura Kim: how expensive is reranking? we have cost constraints.
[03:50] Diego Martinez: reranking adds an extra model call typically with a cheaper embedding/encoder model for scoring, so it's less than full gen but not free. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and cost tradeoffs — we'll include cost estimates in the price sheet.
[04:05] Sophie Turner: for the large regression run you propose, what's the sample size and timeline?
[04:09] Diego Martinez: we'll run 1,000 examples across your current prompt set and the tuned set, log failures, and provide a diff of tokens/cost and F1 precision recall by intent. i can get that done by next tuesday (2026-03-17) if you share the sample dataset.
[04:24] Laura Kim: i'll upload the 1k later today but note some of them contain PHI — will that be ok for your eval infra?
[04:29] Maya Chen: for anything PHI we prefer you sanitize or run through our Private trial environment with VPC. alternatively, we can run the eval on-prem with a sanitized subset. we'll follow up on the exact process in email.
[04:41] Raj Patel: aside from quality, what are the SLA and pricing implications of going dedicated? can you send a top-line comparison?
[04:48] Maya Chen: yes, i'll send a dedicated vs hosted cost sheet and a recommended GPU topology. quick note: reserved capacity gives better predictability and lower unit price, we can include burst capacity options.
[04:58] Diego Martinez: also worth noting quantization profiles — for throughput you can get 20-30% cost reduction with int8 or 4-bit, but that can affect certain clinical QA outputs; we'll recommend which model variants to test.
[05:12] Sophie Turner: any known regressions from quantization we should watch for?
[05:15] Diego Martinez: rare but usually around fine-grained numeric reasoning. we'll flag tests for those.
[05:22] Laura Kim: ok, any open compliance questions?
[05:24] Maya Chen: action item — we'll share SOC2 report, data-flow diagrams, KMS integration doc and audit log schema by tomorrow EOD.
[05:32] Raj Patel: good. also please include the contact for our account engineer for VPC setup.
[05:36] Maya Chen: will do.
[05:38] Diego Martinez: quick note on monitoring: Redwood Console exposes per-route token cost and latency breakdowns; you can set regression alerts tied to your eval prompt sets — we can set that up during the pilot.
[05:51] Laura Kim: that sounds useful. can we do an automatic regression alert on support intent precision falling below 82%?
[05:58] Diego Martinez: yes, thresholds are configurable; we'll add that to the runbook.
[06:04] Maya Chen: ok recap — Diego will run the 1k regression with the new prompt set and return failure cases by 2026-03-17; Laura will provide the 1k sample (sanitized or indicate PHI); Maya will send pricing + SOC2/KMS docs by 2026-03-13; Raj to confirm VPC peering windows by 2026-03-16. we'll schedule a benchmark session week of 2026-03-23.
[06:24] Sophie Turner: thanks all.
[06:26] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with the shared artifacts. bye.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional mis-heard acronyms (k-v cache transcribed as k v stash earlier), speaker overlap near minute 3 produced short crosstalk.

References shared during call: eval spreadsheet link (internal): https://redwood.app/drive/evals/skyline-2026-03-11, SOC2 & KMS docs (will be emailed), pricing sheet (will be attached).
